case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause forbids a State from terminating parental rights on a mere preponderance of the evidence and requires proof by at least clear and convincing evidence.
key_cases.relevance: Santosky supplies the federal constitutional floor that Arkansas codified in Ark. Code Ann. § 9-27-341: no termination order may rest on less than clear and convincing evidence.
key_cases.quote: Evaluation of the three Eldridge factors compels the conclusion that use of a "fair preponderance of the evidence" standard in such proceedings is inconsistent with due process.

key_cases.case_name: Earls v. Ark. Dep't of Human Servs. & Minor Children
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed termination on the subsequent-factors ground, holding that evidence of potential harm combined with the children's adoptability supported the best-interest finding.
key_cases.relevance: It is the operative Arkansas Supreme Court statement of how the two best-interest factors, likelihood of adoption and potential harm, are applied, including to an incarcerated parent.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that the evidence of potential harm, combined with the children's adoptability, supports the circuit court's ruling that termination of Earls's parental rights is in the twins' best interest

key_cases.case_name: Brumley v. Ark. Dep't of Human Servs.
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed termination but agreed with the incarcerated father that incarceration predating the petition could not itself be a 'subsequent factor,' affirming instead on other grounds supported by the record.
key_cases.relevance: It is the leading Arkansas authority limiting the use of a parent's pre-existing incarceration as a termination ground.
key_cases.quote: incarceration alone cannot be a subsequent factor because his incarceration predated the dependency-neglect petition

key_cases.case_name: Myers v. Arkansas Department of Human Services
key_cases.holding: In one of the Tony Alamo Christian Ministries appeals, the court affirmed termination, holding that a termination order requires clear and convincing proof both of best interest and of at least one statutory ground.
key_cases.relevance: It states the two-part clear-and-convincing structure of Ark. Code Ann. § 9-27-341 that every Arkansas termination order must satisfy.
key_cases.quote: Additionally, the trial court must find by clear and convincing evidence that one or more statutory grounds for termination exists.

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed an adoption without the mother's consent after jurisdiction was transferred from Michigan, holding that Arkansas law applied to conduct predating the transfer and that her failure to communicate for over a year was without justifiable cause.
key_cases.relevance: It supplies the Arkansas definition of the one-year failure-to-communicate ground that dispenses with a parent's consent to adoption under Ark. Code Ann. § 9-9-207.
key_cases.quote: Failure to communicate without justifiable cause means a failure that is voluntary, willful, arbitrary, and without adequate excuse.

key_cases.case_name: Bearden v. Arkansas Department of Human Services
key_cases.holding: On review of a court of appeals decision that had reversed, the court affirmed the termination, holding that the chancellor did not clearly err in finding clear and convincing evidence that the mother repeatedly failed to correct the conditions causing removal and that the children, after two years of uncertainty, needed the permanency the termination procedure exists to provide.
key_cases.relevance: This is the most-cited Arkansas statement of how a termination finding is reviewed, and the source Martin, Earls and Brumley all trace back to for the clearly-erroneous review of a clear-and-convincing finding.
key_cases.quote: In reviewing the trial court's evaluation of the evidence, we will not reverse unless the court's finding of clear and convincing evidence is clearly erroneous.

state_agency.name: Arkansas Department of Human Services, Division of Children and Family Services

extended_foster_care_age: Up to age 21 (voluntary; conditions apply — school, job training, 80+ work hours a month, or a documented medical condition; Ark. Code Ann. § 9-27-306)

common_failures: Failure to prove unfitness by clear and convincing evidence
Santosky v. Kramer standard not met

timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Must file TPR or document compelling reason
